inline.s: The Buddha said in the Great Prajñā Sutra that no matter what dharmas there are, all are gathered up within prajñā. Hence among all sutras prajñā is the most essential, and the Diamond Sutra is the most essential part of prajñā. Whatever is essential in the Great Prajñā Sutra is fully present in this sutra. It is clear, then, that reading this sutra is no different from reading the Great Prajñā Sutra; indeed it is no different from reading the whole Tripiṭaka of twelve divisions. What this one sutra teaches is precisely the Dharma of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Hence it says that all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. "All Buddhas" means those who realize it; "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" means the Dharma that is realized. Seen in this light, the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood lies in this sutra, and the attainment of Buddhahood likewise lies in this sutra. One who can receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of Buddhahood and give it away in giving has merit and virtue that cannot be exhausted though one spoke for a whole kalpa. How could the giving of the seven treasures of a trichiliocosm possibly compare? This is the first comparison in this sutra, and the story of the Great Brahma Heaven King is brought in as exactly the right measure. For that was the giving that makes one a Great Brahma Heaven King, while this is the giving that makes one a Buddha. What the Buddha governs is likewise a trichiliocosm. Comparing that with this is quite apt. Yet the Great Brahma Heaven King is still an ordinary being, whereas the Buddha is a sage and the teacher of gods and humans. How could they be compared? Moreover, the Great Brahma Heaven King cannot even escape the three great calamities.

There is a further essential point. This sutra everywhere teaches people not to dwell in marks; this is precisely to make people realize the nature. It is clear, then, that whatever this sutra teaches is the nature. "All come forth from this sutra" really means, without any difference, that this sutra comes forth from the essence of the nature; and because it comes forth from the essence of the nature, people are taught that they must not dwell in marks. The affliction of ordinary people is that they cling everywhere: if not to this, then to that. This sutra everywhere teaches people to see the nature. Yet in the sutra the word "nature" appears nowhere except in the phrase "the nature of merit and virtue is not merit and virtue." The intent is to make people grasp it well for themselves, so that they do not cling even to the word "nature." "All Buddhas come forth from this sutra" also points out to us who study the Buddhadharma that we must enter through this sutra.
This section, which concludes the comparison of merit and virtue and sets forth non-dwelling as the way to generate faith, is most fitting. For faith is the gate of entry to the path.
(Ren) 4. Concluding in freedom from marks.
["Subhūti, what are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma."]

In the early Qing dynasty someone added, after "are not Buddha and Dharma," the line "are called Buddha and Dharma." This is a great mistake. Not using "are called" and saying only "are not" carries deep meaning; how could one add it recklessly? That no such phrase is added here serves to annotate the preceding text. To add it would both violate the style and miss the meaning. Whenever the phrase "are called" is added, it is to open up the following text. Here "Buddha and Dharma" refer to "all Buddhas" above, and "Dharma" to "the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas" above. The Buddha's meaning is: all Buddhas and their supreme enlightenment Dharma as I have spoken of them above are spoken in terms of name and mark; they are not spoken in terms of the nature. This sutra plainly teaches people not to dwell in marks; thus even the two lines above about all Buddhas must not be clung to as marks. If one clings to them as marks, they are not the Buddhas' supreme enlightenment Dharma. Concluded in this way, the meanings of the preceding passages on giving while not dwelling in marks, on not grasping dharmas and not grasping non-dharmas, are all brought to perfection.

The section above on showing non-dwelling in order to generate faith, from its opening words, has one give the vast deliverance of beings to Buddhahood (entering nirvāṇa without residue is precisely attaining Buddhahood); this shows us that we should not dwell in the marks of self and others. It then says, "in truth there are no beings who attain deliverance," which means we should not dwell in the marks of dharmas. It further says, "dwelling in no dharma, practice giving and the other dharmas," which means we should not dwell in the marks of non-dharmas. And so the four words "not dwelling in marks" sum it all up. Not dwelling in marks is the true explanation of non-dwelling. The reason we should not dwell is to subdue the deluded mind. (The deluded mind is consciousness, that is, discrimination.) The deluded mind is nothing else: it means discriminating and clinging to marks. Yet in the question, dwelling comes first and subduing second; in the answer, subduing comes first and dwelling second. And when answering about dwelling, it says, "should dwell in non-dwelling," and again, "should dwell only as taught." But what was taught is precisely non-dwelling. Is this not to say that one should dwell in non-dwelling? This again plainly shows that one need only remove delusion, and should not go seeking further for the true. For when delusion is removed, the true appears of itself. Moreover, the nature of true thusness is thus, equal and impartial. If one were to dwell in the true, one would fall into clinging to difference. Clinging becomes delusion; what truth would remain? Difference is not equality; what thusness would remain? Therefore one should only use non-dwelling to subdue delusion; this itself is right dwelling. How could one seek a dwelling place elsewhere? When one part of delusion is removed, one part of the true appears; why seek the true separately? Hence it follows: "All marks are delusive." This clarifies the fault of dwelling in marks. If one dwells in marks, one follows delusion. This is why subduing is spoken of first. Again it says: "If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathāgata." This clarifies the benefit of not dwelling in marks. If one can avoid dwelling in the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas, one sees the true nature. This is why it speaks only of subduing and not of dwelling, since subduing is itself right dwelling. Such an exposition is plainly evident. That is why all the passages above are gathered into one small section and entitled "Clear Indication."

Such a clear indication is given in order to enable people to generate faith, and so it is followed by the small section on generating faith. Here precept-keeping and merit-cultivation alone are singled out as able to generate faith, and this carries especially profound meaning. To speak briefly, there are three points.

(1) Prajñā here means right wisdom, and wisdom is born of concentration, while concentration is perfected by precepts. Now if one wishes to open right wisdom, one must keep the precepts. Otherwise right wisdom does not arise, and instead one develops mad wisdom and walks into wrong paths, in the greatest danger. The two wheels of merit and wisdom cannot lack either one. Only when both wheels roll together does one become the honored twofold body. If wisdom is great and merit small, then great compassion is lacking, and one cannot gather and transform beings. Therefore, in cultivating prajñā-wisdom one cannot cultivate it apart from giving and the other pāramitās. Thus the sutra says at its beginning, "deliver all beings," and again, "dwelling in no dharma, practice giving." To cultivate wisdom apart from merit means having no karmic connection with beings, and the marks of excellence are also incomplete. Even if one wished to transform beings, they would not listen to one's teaching. This is something we must understand.

(2) Keeping the precepts, one has few desires and knows contentment. Cultivating merit, one must deeply believe in cause and effect. Now as one cultivates the prajñā of contemplation, if craving is great, how can one leave marks behind? If cause and effect are unclear, one easily falls into the mark of annihilation. The sutra says that those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can generate faith. This plainly shows that we should keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and only then can we enter the gate of prajñā. For faith is the gate of entry to the path. Its warning is deep and urgent. This, again, we must understand. In short, one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit is already free of the mark of non-dharmas. Therefore, contemplating emptiness of self and emptiness of dharmas in accord with the sutra, one will by no means step onto a wrong path. If one thought truly corresponds, one immediately enters the principle of the three emptinesses: what is called having no marks of self and others, no marks of dharmas, and no marks of non-dharmas.

What is called "no" is not stubborn emptiness; it means not grasping marks. The two words "not grasping" are again the true explanation of not dwelling in marks. And if one wishes not to grasp marks, one should not grasp dharmas and should not grasp non-dharmas. To grasp dharmas is to form the mark of dharma, that is, to cling to existence. To grasp non-dharmas is to form the mark of non-dharma, that is, to cling to emptiness. Not clinging to either emptiness or existence is the middle path and the ultimate meaning; it is the Dharma of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. It is like a raft: while crossing, one relies on it; once across, one should still let it go. Therefore, though one has already become a Buddha, though one teaches the Dharma and delivers beings as a Buddha does, one attains without possessing what one attains, and speaks without possessing what one speaks. One cannot fixate on there being dharmas, nor fixate on there being no dharmas. Hence it says, "There is no fixed dharma." These four words are again the true explanation of not grasping dharmas and not grasping non-dharmas. They show that because there is nothing fixed, one should not grasp. What is called not grasping means simply not clinging. In short, whatever the Buddha teaches is from the outset ungraspable and unutterable. One must enter it where mental activity ceases and the path of words is cut off. Therefore to grasp dharmas and teach dharmas, to grasp non-dharmas and teach non-dharmas, are both wrong. This is called the unconditioned. Nirvāṇa, whether one aspires to sagehood or to Buddhahood, is reached by none other than this. Understanding this true meaning is true faith. One thought corresponding brings immeasurable merit and virtue. For one thought corresponding is the root of continuous pure mindfulness.

How is the merit and virtue immeasurable? Again, a small section comparing and surpassing makes its reason clear. It is as said: all Buddhas and the supreme enlightenment of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. This explains that all Buddhas and all Buddhadharmas are not outside the principle of non-dwelling taught in this sutra. If one truly believes this principle, then with one pure thought one can go straight to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Is the merit and virtue then not immeasurable? Yet one must not, on hearing these words, seek it in the words and text. One must rely on the principle made clear in the sutra and turn the light back upon one's own nature. The nature is empty and still; there is no word "Buddha" and no word "Dharma" in it. If one can contemplate thus for a long time and realize and enter the empty, still nature, then one has accomplished unsurpassed enlightenment; then one has become a Buddha. Yet though the Buddha has become a Buddha, he never thinks that there is the slightest dharma to be attained. To have not the slightest dharma to be attained is not to think that one has become a Buddha. Hence it says, "What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma." From beginning to end, one thread runs through it all: non-dwelling, and nothing more. The cause embraces the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. Thus, thus.

The above is the gist of the first section, showing non-dwelling; it is already detailed and complete. Our World-Honored One, in great kindness and compassion, wishing people to open wide a perfect understanding, again presses the meaning of non-dwelling forward layer by layer and makes it clear, hoping that when the wisdom of understanding is opened, the root of faith will be accomplished and the work of cultivation will grow accordingly.

(Geng) Next, pressing forward and unfolding non-dwelling in order to open understanding. It divides into five: (Xin) 1. Extensively explaining by way of the fruition; 2. Explaining in detail by way of the cause; 3. Asking for the name and its upholding; 4. Accomplishing the wisdom of understanding; 5. Fully revealing the merit of the sutra.

This section, pressing forward and unfolding non-dwelling in order to open understanding, again divides into five small sections. The first is explaining extensively by way of the fruition. It runs from the ninth part to the first three lines of the tenth part. Explaining extensively by way of the fruition carries on from the words above, that all sages and worthies are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma, and proves this by citing an example. It also echoes from afar the passages on not grasping dharmas or non-dharmas, on being ungraspable and unutterable, and on the Buddhadharma being no Buddhadharma: attaining yet not attaining, which is not grasping dharmas, is what is called the Buddhadharma being no Buddhadharma; not attaining yet attaining, which is not grasping non-dharmas, is what is called the Buddhadharma. To attain without anything attained, and not to attain is precisely to attain: mental activity is extinguished and words are cut off. What can be grasped? What can be spoken? All of this makes clear the meaning of not dwelling on either side. If it is so in the fruition, it can be known in the cause; if it is so for the Small Vehicle, all the more can it be known for the Great Vehicle.

blocks.text: One Mark Without Marks, Part Nine

inline.s: (Xin) 1. This divides into two: (Ren) 1. Discussing the four fruits in general; 2. Teacher and disciple proving and confirming. (Ren) 1. Again divides into four: (Gui) 1. Making clear that the first fruit is free from marks; 2. Making clear that the second fruit is free from marks; 3. Making clear that the third fruit is free from marks; 4. Making clear that the fourth fruit is free from marks.
(Gui) 1. Making clear that the first fruit is free from marks.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can a srota-āpanna think, 'I have attained the fruit of srota-āpanna'?" Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why? A srota-āpanna is called a stream-enterer, yet he enters nothing; he does not enter forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, or dharmas. Therefore he is called a srota-āpanna."]

The first fruit cuts off completely the eighty-eight afflictions of the three realms, and one has already seen the principle of true emptiness and knows that there is no self and no belonging to a self. If one gave rise to the thought "I can attain the fruit," the view of self would still be there; how could one be said to have attained the fruit? The second fruit and above follow this pattern. Subhūti explains in each case by way of the names and marks of the four fruits, so that one who clings to the mark of fruition may at once, on the spot, feel utterly at a loss. Such is the skill of his teaching. ("No" is a live phrase; it is like saying it is not that there is no attainment, but that one cannot form such a thought. The word "called" in "is called" means a provisional name, not something to be pinned down as real. To pin it down is precisely to form a thought and cling to something attained.)

The Sanskrit word srota-āpanna means "stream-enterer," that is, one who has already entered the stream that leads to nirvāṇa. By following this stream back to its source, one can reach the other shore of nirvāṇa. Yet though he is called a stream-enterer, he in truth enters nothing. The phrase "he does not enter" explains precisely why. For when faculties and objects stand over against each other, this is called the six entries, meaning that faculties and objects enter into one another. (For instance, when the eye meets a form, it is as if the form entered the eye, and the eye is turned about by the form. This may also be called the eye entering into form. The rest follow this pattern.) The reason they enter into one another is that consciousness discriminates. Now the sutra says he does not enter, showing that he is able to empty emotional consciousness. Because he does not enter the six objects, there is no way to name him, so he is named a stream-enterer. And again, because he does not enter the six objects and emotional consciousness is able to be emptied, though he is called a stream-enterer, he in truth enters nothing. This is merely the provisional name "stream-enterer." Hence it says, "is called a srota-āpanna." "Name" means provisional name, name and mark. The phrase "is called" below follows the same pattern. The sense is: if one formed the thought "I can enter the stream," then plainly there would be something entered, and if there were something entered, emotional consciousness would still be there; how could one be said to have attained the first fruit? In short, attaining the fruit comes precisely from having no thought; to form a thought is then not to attain the fruit.
(Gui) 2. Making clear that the second fruit is free from marks.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can a sakṛdāgāmin think, 'I have attained the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin'?" Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why? A sakṛdāgāmin is called one who returns once, yet in truth he does not return. Therefore he is called a sakṛdāgāmin."]

The Sanskrit word sakṛdāgāmin means "one who returns once." Having realized the first fruit, one advances and cuts off the delusions of craving in the desire realm, from the highest of the high down to the middle of the low, six grades in all. Three lower grades still remain. (The delusions of craving in the desire realm number nine grades. When the fifth grade is cut off, that is, up to the middle of the middle grade, one is called a candidate for the second fruit. When the sixth grade is cut off, one is said to have attained the second fruit.) One must go once to the heavens and come once to the human realm to cut them off; hence one is called "one who returns once." Yet in his mind there is in truth not even the mark of returning. Because he has no mark of returning, he is able to return once. And because he has not even the mark of returning, how could there be a difference between returning once and returning twice? This too is merely the provisional name "one who returns once." The sense is: if one formed the thought "I return once," then plainly one would cling to the mark of returning. Since one already clings to marks, there is plainly discrimination. The first fruit could not then be attained; how could one be said to have attained the second fruit?
(Gui) 3. Making clear that the third fruit is free from marks.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can an anāgāmin think, 'I have attained the fruit of anāgāmin'?" Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why? An anāgāmin is called one who does not return, yet in truth he does not come. Therefore he is called an anāgāmin."]

The Sanskrit word anāgāmin means "one who does not return." Having realized the second fruit, one advances and cuts off completely the three lower grades of delusion of craving in the desire realm. One then dwells in the four dhyāna heavens of the form realm and does not return to the human realm; hence one is called "one who does not return." Yet in his mind there is in truth no such thing as coming. Because the thought of coming is already gone, he is able not to return. And because he has not even the notion of coming, how could there be any notion of not returning? This too is merely the provisional name "not returning." The sense is: if one formed the thought "I do not return," then plainly coming and not coming would still not be lightly forgotten. If not wholly forgotten, emotional consciousness is still present; this should not be found even in one who has attained the first fruit, let alone one said to have attained the third fruit.
(Gui) 4. Making clear that the fourth fruit is free from marks.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can an arhat think, 'I have attained the way of the arhat'?" Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why? There is in truth no dharma called an arhat. World-Honored One, if an arhat formed the thought 'I have attained the way of the arhat,' he would be clinging to self, person, being, and life."]

The Sanskrit word arhat means "no birth." Having realized the third fruit, one cuts off in the four dhyāna heavens all seventy-two grades of delusion of craving of the two upper realms and thereupon realizes the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and does not receive further existence. Birth and death are thereby ended; hence one is called "no birth." Yet in his mind there is in truth not even a dharma. Because there is no dharma, the mind of birth and death comes to rest; hence it is called no birth. And because he has not even a dharma of no birth, how could there be any such thing as no birth? This too is merely the provisional name "no birth." The sense is: if one formed the thought "no birth," then plainly there would be a dharma. Since there is a mark of dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life. One's mind stirs and thoughts arise, and one is still an ordinary being. How could one be said to have attained the fourth fruit and realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas?

(Ren) 2. Proving and confirming by teacher and disciple. It divides into two: (Gui) 1. By way of the one at hand, showing no attainment; 2. By way of a past cause, showing no attainment. (Gui) 1. Again divides into three: (Zi) 1. Quoting the Buddha's words; 2. Stating freedom from marks; 3. Explaining why.
(Zi) 1. Quoting the Buddha's words.
["World-Honored One, the Buddha said that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention, and that I am foremost among men, the foremost arhat free from desire.

Non-contention means not competing with anything, the meaning of total equality. Because one does not insist on being right, one can be free of contention. Free of contention, one does not trouble others. The intent is to guard others' minds and keep them from giving rise to affliction. To cultivate this samādhi, is it not great kindness? Yet the reason this samādhi is accomplished is that the marks of self, person, right, and wrong are all empty. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: Subhūti dwells in the ground of empty space. If a being resents me for standing, I will sit upright all day without rising; if he resents me for sitting, I will stand all day without moving. It is clear that because he dwells in emptiness, he is able to be like this. The elder was foremost in understanding emptiness, and so he could enter this samādhi. (The ten great disciples each had their own specialty, and each was called foremost. Mahākāśyapa was foremost in ascetic practices; Ānanda in much hearing; others such as Śāriputra in wisdom, Maudgalyāyana in supernormal powers, Rāhula in secret practices, Aniruddha in the divine eye, Pūrṇa in teaching the Dharma, Kātyāyana in debate, Upāli in upholding the precepts, and Subhūti in understanding emptiness, were all foremost.) Samādhi here means right reception, also called right concentration. Not receiving any reception is called right reception. When one receives nothing at all, one is not moved by anything; this is right concentration. People say he is an ordinary being. Ordinary beings delight in contention; how could they be free of contention? Hence it says, "foremost among men." The word "desire" in its broad sense refers to all deluded craving. Only when one has cut off completely the afflictions of greed and so forth in the three realms is one truly free from desire. No one who becomes an arhat is not free from desire. Freedom from desire also necessarily means not competing with anything; but without having attained the samādhi of non-contention, the elder is nevertheless allowed the title of foremost. The verse says: "Relying on that Subhūti, one speaks of freedom from the two obstacles." (The New Eye Commentary takes the delusions of view and craving as the two obstacles, which is too narrow.) The ancient commentary says that freedom from desire means freedom from the obstacle of afflictions, which is shared by all arhats. (Delusions of view and delusions of craving are together called afflictions.) Though he attained the samādhi of non-contention, he did not keep the notion of having attained anything (that is, he forgot himself that he was free of contention); he forgot himself that he was in this concentration. This is freedom from the obstacle of samādhi. Thus he truly attained non-contention and truly attained the samādhi. Hence he is called the foremost arhat free from desire. Joined with the previous line, it means that not only is he foremost among all men, but even speaking of an arhat's freedom from desire, he is called foremost. These are the World-Honored One's usual words of praise for the elder; hence "the Buddha said." Since the elder had himself forgotten that he was in this concentration, and the other disciples could not reach it either, only the one fully enlightened could know that he had entered this samādhi; hence only the Buddha could say it. "Buddha" is the title of the fully enlightened. This section precisely sets out his meritorious conduct and marks, and does not discuss freedom from marks. (The next section is where freedom from marks is stated.) Hence it does not say "the Tathāgata said" but "the Buddha said." For the Tathāgata is the title of the virtue of the nature. Speaking in terms of the nature, then names and marks such as non-contention and foremost cannot be spoken of at all. In this sutra not even a single form of address is without wondrous meaning. Thus, thus.
(Zi) 2. Stating freedom from marks.
["I do not form the thought that I am an arhat free from desire."]

The circulating editions have the two words "World-Honored One" here; the manuscript sutras and ancient editions do not, and it may be omitted. The two lines of sutra text here are easy to understand. What should now be said is this: the elder says only "arhat free from desire" and does not say "samādhi of non-contention," and this too has a wondrous meaning. For it precisely makes clear that he had forgotten himself that he was in this concentration. Moreover, in ordinary freedom from desire one does not even keep the notion of having attained anything. That he did not think himself to have attained the samādhi of non-contention can then be known.
(Zi) 3. Explaining why. It divides into two: (Chou) 1. Reverse demonstration; 2. Direct statement.
(Chou) 1. Reverse demonstration.
["World-Honored One, if I formed the thought, 'I have attained the way of the arhat,' the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti delights in dwelling in quietness."]

In the line "if I formed the thought," only the Zhao commentary edition lacks the word "I." Since the next line has "I," it may originally be omitted here; but the present editions follow the manuscript sutra throughout, and so it is retained. "The way of the arhat" means precisely freedom from desire. Araṇya here means quietude, also called freedom from affairs. (Meaning the marks of affairs.) When marks are exhausted without and the mind is stilled within, inner and outer are both quiescent, and there is no time that is not still. This is another name for the samādhi of non-contention. "Walker" means one's practice. "Delights" means to be fond of, the sense of the mind being in accord and united with it. For to be fond of it to the utmost is called delight, with the sense of staking one's very life on it. "Delighting in the practice of quietness" means that mind and practice are in accord without interval, that is, the sense of having realized it. The previous line does not say "freedom from desire" but instead says "the way of the arhat," and the next line does not say "the samādhi of non-contention" but instead says "delights in the practice of quietness," because the meanings of the two names are exactly the same. (Arhat means no birth, meaning that the one mind does not arise. Araṇya means inner and outer both quiescent, which is likewise the sense that the one mind does not arise.) Thus the point that to keep a notion of attainment is then not truly to attain becomes all the more plainly evident. With this reverse demonstration, the meanings stated above, that one who has marks of self and so forth is not a bodhisattva, and that grasping marks is clinging to marks of self and so forth, are further clarified. Why is it that clinging to self makes one not a bodhisattva? Because one's practice is wholly lost. If a thought arises in the mind, there must be grasping. Grasping forms a mark, and that mark is self, person, being, and life. The reason a thought arises is nothing else: one has not forgotten one's attachment to the one who attains and what is attained. The one who attains is then the mark of self, and what is attained is the mark of person. (Who is the one who attains? The self; hence the attainer belongs to self. Set over against the attainer is the attained, just as set over against self is person; hence the attained is the mark of person.) That attainer and attained are not one is the mark of being; holding to them without interruption is the mark of life. To form one thought of attainment is then not to attain. One may know that to form even one thought of giving and so forth is then not to give. Then one who brings forth the great mind and practices the great practice must by no means dwell in marks; this is clear. For if one who gives keeps the notion of what is given, he most easily becomes self-satisfied and complacent; could he still practice giving widely? The rest may be known by analogy.
(Chou) 2. Direct statement.
["Because Subhūti in truth practices nothing, he is called one who delights in the practice of quietness."]

In the direct statement, the phrase "in truth practices nothing" is to be understood as "in truth has nothing that he practices," meaning that he practices yet has nothing practiced. The meaning of "nothing attained" is likewise so. It must not be misread as "practices nothing at all" or "attains nothing at all."

This section carries on from the one above. It should have said "in truth attains nothing." Yet here it says "in truth practices nothing," and there is deep meaning in this. For it means that because in practicing this practice he had nothing practiced, he is called one who delights in the practice of quietness. In other words, it is because he had nothing practiced that he was then able to realize it. This makes all those on the causal ground tremble when they hear it. If one cannot be free of marks through non-dwelling, then this cultivation is in vain. The fruition stages were cited above precisely to serve as a mirror for those on the causal ground. Now that the Small Vehicle fruition stages have been fully stated, it is especially said that he in truth practices nothing in order to wake them up. It does not say "because I in truth practice nothing" but "because Subhūti," and this too contains deep meaning. For it shows that what is called "in truth practices nothing" is seen by an onlooker, while the person himself has forgotten that he in truth practices nothing. The sense is that even "in truth practices nothing" cannot be kept in the mind. To keep it is to dwell in marks. Why? For the mind's keeping it is the mind's grasping. If the mind grasps marks, then one clings to self, person, being, and life. Further, weighing its tone, it seems to speak on the World-Honored One's behalf. The sense is that the World-Honored One said Subhūti delights in the practice of quietness for no other reason than that Subhūti in truth practices nothing. And the word "called" also has meaning. It makes one know that delighting in the practice of quietness also belongs to name and mark. In the nature, not even this phrase can be fastened.

Looking over the meaning of the several sections above: all of them make clear that one must attain yet have nothing attained in order truly to attain. If there is something attained, then it is not attainment. They make those on the causal ground know that one must practice yet have nothing practiced in order truly to practice. If there is something practiced, then it is not practice. How is it to have nothing attained and nothing practiced? By not forming thoughts. Not forming thoughts precisely points out the guiding principle of not grasping and not dwelling. Knowing this, non-dwelling at last has a place of entry. All of this is what he wished to make clear.

blocks.text: Adorning the Pure Land, Part Ten

inline.s: (Gui) 2. By way of a past cause, showing no attainment.

[The Buddha told Subhūti, "What do you think? In the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he attain any dharma?" "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he in truth attained no dharma."]

This concerns the World-Honored One in former times, when he was practicing the bodhisattva path and had just ascended to the eighth ground. Looking ahead to his later attainment of perfect enlightenment, it is still the causal ground. But looking back from those who have just brought forth the mind, it is a fruition stage. This matter is cited here and spoken for the sake of those who bring forth the unsurpassed bodhi mind. Hence this section on a past cause is also classified within the extensive explanation by way of the fruition.

The affair of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, and of his bestowing the prediction on the World-Honored One as his own teacher, is found in the Abhiniṣkramaṇa Sutra and the Sutra of Auspicious Omens. (Before Dīpaṃkara left home, his original name was Dīpaṃkara, "Lamp-bearer." A lamp with a foot is called a stand-lamp; without a foot, a lamp. He was so named because when he was born everything around him was like lamplight.) The World-Honored One was then a bodhisattva of the seventh ground (named Ru Tong, also called Shan Hui), just at the point when the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa of cultivation was about to be completed. Meeting the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and ascended to the eighth ground. (Thereupon he entered the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.) Dīpaṃkara then gave him the prediction, saying: after ninety-one kalpas from now, in the kalpa named Worthies, you shall attain Buddhahood with the name Śākyamuni. The non-arising of dharmas means true suchness, the mark of reality. "Acceptance" means penetrating without obstruction and not retreating. It is what is called principle and wisdom merging, accepted, sealed, and upheld. There are various accounts of realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas in the Great Vehicle. The Treatise on Wisdom says it is obtained on ascending the grounds (speaking in terms of the distinct teaching). Sutras such as the Benevolent King say it is obtained on the seventh, eighth, or ninth ground. One should know that in the perfect teaching it is already partly realized from the first abiding onward. (What is called breaking one part of ignorance and realizing one part of the dharma-body.) As for the eighth ground, there it is realized completely, and so one is called beyond training. Even up to equal enlightenment, seeing the nature is like gazing at the moon through gauze. Only in perfect enlightenment is it realized ultimately.

The "dharma" in "any dharma" is explained in all the commentaries as the words of the prediction, which is not quite apt. Only Ouyi explains it as the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, which is most correct. (The commentaries are, it seems, stuck on Maitreya's verse. The verse says: "The Buddha's words to Dīpaṃkara did not grasp principle or true wisdom; by this true meaning, that non-grasping teaching was accomplished." Note that the word "words" in the verse does not point specifically to the words of the prediction. The World-Honored One in the past realized non-arising through hearing the Dharma, and so the prediction was given. Thus the word "words" in the verse seems to refer to the Dharma words spoken by Dīpaṃkara. The sense of the verse is that he heard the Dharma words and did not grasp at the principle-essence or at true wisdom. (As distinct from provisional wisdom, hence "true wisdom.") For this reason the true meaning was accomplished. From this one may prove that he (the World-Honored One) certainly did not grasp at what Dīpaṃkara said. (This line carries the sense of the verse's line on the elder's attaining nothing.) In short, because he did not cling to principle and wisdom, he was able to merge principle and wisdom and realize non-arising. "True meaning" refers to non-arising. The non-arising of dharmas is true suchness, the mark of reality, hence "true meaning.") Or it may refer to the Dharma heard while with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, and that is also acceptable. "Attained something" means having what is attained. To have what is attained is to grasp and to dwell in marks. The question means: when he heard the Dharma then, could he be free from dwelling in marks? If we speak in terms of realizing the acceptance of non-arising, then the word "attain" is still easier to understand. It asks: when he formerly attained the non-arising of dharmas, was there in his mind a non-arising of dharmas that was attained? It does not say "formed the thought," because to have what is attained is precisely to form a thought, and so it is omitted. Though the World-Honored One asks in order to probe, he has in fact already secretly handed over the golden needle; from the first he says "the Tathāgata." Speaking in terms of the nature, the Dharma has no form at all; from where could attainment come? What follows the World-Honored One is the elder's words, as may be seen from the two words "World-Honored One." In sutra editions after the Song, there is "No" before "World-Honored One," which is a great error. Whenever the word "No" is followed by text, it is a live phrase. Looking at the answer below, it is a definitive statement; why would this live phrase be needed? The elder too begins by saying "the Tathāgata," exactly matching the question point for point. That it was a case of nothing attained needs no further words. How did the elder know that he in truth attained no dharma, and make this definitive statement? Because if one dwells in marks while hearing the Dharma, then birth and death in the mind are not yet at rest; how could one at once realize non-arising? So one knows that when he heard the teaching then, he in truth had nothing attained. This explains it by way of hearing the Dharma. If one explains it by way of realizing the non-arising of dharmas: since he realized the non-arising of dharmas, how could he keep any notion of attainment? If there were a single non-arising of dharmas that was attained, that would still be a mind of birth and death. Could that be called realizing the non-arising of dharmas? So one knows that though he attained the non-arising of dharmas, in this dharma he in truth had nothing attained.

The explanation of the meaning according to the text above is now complete. But the overall meaning of this section contains especially subtle depths, which one must not fail to know. What is the overall meaning? It is why this section is spoken again at all. Let me divide it roughly into three parts.

The sections above have already fully set forth the meaning of attaining the fruit without dwelling. Those on the causal ground should be able to understand clearly that they must not dwell. Yet one must still guard against the thought that although cause and fruition must be one and the same, and fruition is thus, therefore the cause should also be thus—yet perhaps the Small Vehicle fruition stages and the Great Vehicle causal practices are not entirely the same. Therefore, after finishing with the Small Vehicle, he especially cites the Great Vehicle fruition stage as well, which likewise is attaining without attaining and must not dwell in marks, to make this clear. This is so that all who cultivate the Great Vehicle may have not the slightest doubt about the principle of non-dwelling. This is the first part.

In speaking of the Great Vehicle fruition stage, he does not cite a Buddha but a bodhisattva. This guards against the doubt that a Buddha is fully enlightened and how could one compare oneself to him. The bodhisattva's position, moreover, stands between cause and fruition. Later in this sutra this same matter is cited again and explained further: if at that time he had attained any dharma, no prediction would have been given; because he attained nothing, the prediction was given. This makes one know that a bodhisattva who dwells in marks cannot become a Buddha. Then one who brings forth the mind and cultivates the Great Vehicle, if he dwells in marks, how could he become a bodhisattva, and how could it be bodhisattva practice? Hence the section above says that one who has marks of self and others is not a bodhisattva. Explained in this way, the principle that cause and fruition are one and the same, and the essential point of non-dwelling, are still more clearly understood. This is the second part.

Citing a bodhisattva fruition stage is all very well. But why cite only the eighth ground and not bodhisattvas of the other grounds? Because the Small Vehicle fruition stages were explained above with those who attain non-arising as having realized the way and as beyond training. So now for the Great Vehicle he likewise cites the eighth ground, where one attains non-arising, up to being beyond training. "Beyond training" means having realized the way. Before the eighth ground, though one has realized, it is not yet complete, so one is called still in training. (As for ultimate realization, that lies in the Buddha's position.) What the Small and Great Vehicles realize is the same. This keeps those who hear from having the slightest doubt about the principle of non-dwelling. Moreover, this sutra says at its opening that one should bring forth the mind to enter nirvāṇa without residue. Later it says that sages and worthies are all distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma. Nirvāṇa and the unconditioned both carry the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing. Therefore for both Vehicles he speaks of those who realize non-arising, exactly corresponding to what was said before. This makes one know that since one has brought forth the mind and wishes to enter non-arising, the mind must not arise or cease. How can the mind be made not to arise? One must certainly not dwell in marks. As soon as there is any dwelling, it is a mind of birth and death; how could one realize and enter non-arising? Therefore non-dwelling is precisely the one and only method of entry into non-arising. This is the third part. Seeing these three meanings, one may know how fine and close this sutra's principles are, and how strictly its threads are woven. The compiler of the sutra prefixed the two words "the Buddha told," precisely to show us that this contains profound meaning, and that it must not be sought merely in the words.

(Xin) 2. Explaining in detail by way of the cause. It divides into two: (Ren) 1. Directly revealing by way of the causal mind; 2. Comparing and revealing by way of the sutra's merit. (Ren) 1. Again divides into three: (Gui) 1. First making clear that adorning lands is non-dwelling; 2. Revealing the accomplishment of bringing forth the non-dwelling mind; 3. Confirming by the non-dwelling of the reward body.
(Gui) 1. First making clear that adorning lands is non-dwelling.
["Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-lands?" "No, World-Honored One. Why? What is called adorning the Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment."]

When a bodhisattva cultivates the cause, the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices, each and every practice, is dedicated to the Pure Land. This is called adorning. What is called "with this merit and virtue, adorning the Buddha's Pure Land" is precisely this. Then how could a bodhisattva not adorn the Buddha-lands? This is raised as a question precisely because he wishes those who cultivate to understand the way of adorning. If one does not get its way, then whatever one adorns is all on the level of marks, having nothing to do with one's own nature, and becomes outflows merit and virtue. This is the deep meaning of raising the question. One should know that in "adorning the Buddha's Pure Land," the word "pure" is most essential. How is a land pure? Through the purity of the mind. Since the mind must be pure, adorning cannot cling to marks; if the mind grasps marks, it is no longer pure. What does this mean? One must understand the meaning of the two lines above, "should not grasp dharmas," before one has the way of true adorning. Why? To adorn while clinging to marks is to grasp dharmas. If one misunderstands the meaning of not clinging to marks and does not adorn at all, that is to grasp non-dharmas. Raising this as a question is precisely to test whether one can truly understand the true meaning of grasping neither side.

Again, the question and answer above, repeatedly citing the fruition virtue of non-dwelling, was originally to make clear that causal practice should also be non-dwelling. Here it speaks directly of causal practice. The bodhisattva who adorns the Buddha-lands is precisely the bodhisattva who brings forth the unsurpassed bodhi mind. To understand the way of adorning lands is to understand the way of giving and the rest. "No" is a live phrase; it is like saying it is not that there is adornment, and not that there is no adornment. "Why?" below explains its meaning. The phrase "what is called adorning the Buddha-lands" is the topic stated. "Is not" makes clear that it does not cling to existence, that is, that one should not grasp dharmas. "Is called" makes clear that it does not cling to emptiness, that is, that one should not grasp non-dharmas. For speaking in terms of the mind-nature: the essence of the nature is empty and still (empty and still is what is called the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth makes clear that it is not a false mark. To realize the ultimate truth, one must be free from marks; hence "is not." "Not" carries the sense of freedom from). How could there be any such thing as adornment? Hence "is not." And speaking in terms of affairs and marks, it can be heard and seen (can be heard and seen is what is called conventional truth. Conventional truth is the marks of the world. Since the provisional exists but is not real, it is called "name"). It is plainly adorned in full; hence "is." The sense is: because its name and marks do exist, one should not cling to emptiness and grasp non-dharmas. The bodhisattva should diligently cultivate the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices to adorn it. Because the mind-nature is originally empty, one should not cling to existence and grasp dharmas. Though the bodhisattva advances diligently in adorning, in his mind it is as if nothing were happening. When the one mind is thus pure, the land is pure of itself. This is what is called adorning the Buddha-lands, and only thus does one get the way of adorning. One should know that cultivating the cause to obtain the fruition, and attaining the surpassing, wondrous reward body and the pure Buddha-land, are all manifested by the mind. And only when the mind is pure can they be manifested. It is like polishing a mirror: when the dust is gone, the image appears. Hence the Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: the wisdom of the great perfect mirror can manifest and produce the wisdom-images of body, land, and wisdom. In short, adorning the Buddha-lands should be neither grasping nor annihilating. "Is not" makes clear that one does not grasp marks. "Is called" makes clear that it is not the mark of annihilation. Again, the moment "is not" is said, "is called" immediately follows, making clear that though it is not, it nonetheless is. The nature must manifest marks; nature and marks have never been apart. If one knows that it is not and yet does not grasp marks, what harm is there in adorning its marks? If one wishes to say "is called" but first says "is not," this makes clear that though it is, it nonetheless is not. For marks fundamentally take the nature as their essence, and marks arise from the nature. Therefore when practicing what is and not annihilating, one should still merge back into the nature. This is the essential gist of the Buddha's question and answer with Subhūti. We must understand this gist and practice according to the teaching.

The two phrases "is not" and "is called" are precisely the essentials of Buddha-recitation. "Is not" makes clear that the self-nature is pure and originally has no thought. "Is called" makes clear that deluded thoughts flourish and one must hold the name in order to remove deluded thoughts. One must recite until there is recitation without recitation and no recitation in recitation, until delusion is exhausted and the mind of thoughts is empty, until the one mind is pure. This is called single-mindedness undistracted, and undistracted is what is called pure. If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
(Gui) 2. Revealing the accomplishment of bringing forth the non-dwelling mind.

["Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus bring forth a pure mind. They should not bring forth a mind dwelling in forms, and should not bring forth a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, or dharmas. They should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever."]

This section has not much sutra text, yet it concludes the preceding text. From the opening words spoken at the start down to the present, it is the spot where the eye is dotted and the vital point is tied for a thousand words and ten thousand phrases. Therefore its meanings are extremely fine and extremely deep. If one merely explains the words and reads it casually, one will fail the Buddha's kindness. Now to explain how it dots the eye and ties the vital point, I must first explain the words. Yet in this short passage of barely two lines, meanings pierce through in every direction and wondrous senses arise in rings; even explaining the words is not easy.

"Therefore" is what is called a word that carries on the above and starts the below. Since it runs through all the explanations that have come before, it not only carries on from adorning lands, and not only carries on from the extensive explanation by way of the fruition, and not only carries on from the section on generating faith within the detailed discussion. It is directly and closely linked in echo with the several lines of general instruction at the opening of the sutra. And first, to speak in terms of the nearby thread: above, the four fruits were first explained, each attaining the fruit without dwelling. Next, Subhūti himself stated that he attained the fruit and likewise did not dwell. These all belong to the Small Vehicle. Then the World-Honored One, by way of his own past, made clear that in regard to dharmas he truly did not dwell. (The sutra says, "in regard to dharmas he in truth attained nothing," which is not dwelling in the dharmas that are attained.) Here it speaks of the Great Vehicle. Yet it still lies between cause and fruition. Finally, by way of the bodhisattva cultivating the six pāramitās, it shows that in adorning the Buddha-lands he likewise does not dwell. "Is not" means not dwelling in the marks of dharmas. "Is called" means not dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas. Here it speaks exclusively of the Great Vehicle causal ground. Thus, sparing no pains, it explains layer by layer, drawing closer and closer. It is nothing but a wish to make clear the "should bring forth a pure mind" and "should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever" of this section. Therefore it uses "therefore" to carry on the above and start the below, making clear that all that was said above serves as a groundwork for bringing forth the mind without dwelling and dwelling without bringing forth the mind. It is also for the sake of good men and good women who bring forth the supreme bodhi mind, pointing out the guiding principle. The extensive explanation by way of the fruition originally carries on from the line "all sages and worthies are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma," and that line in turn concludes what was said before. Hence this section is linked in echo with the lines at the opening about good men and good women. "All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas" are the bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas spoken of at the opening of the sutra, that is, the good men and good women who bring forth the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment mind and ask how they should dwell and how they should subdue. "Should" is a word of decision. Whether Small or Great Vehicle, fruition stage or causal ground, all should not dwell. One may know that those who bring forth the great mind should certainly also not dwell. It cannot be otherwise; hence "should."

This section's text both carries on the above and starts the below. Therefore the two words "thus" point to both the preceding and the following text. To speak of only one side would leave the meaning incomplete. First, let us explain it as pointing to the text below. It points precisely to the line "should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever," and the two "should not" lines are also included. One should know that the two lines "should not dwell in forms" are the premise of the line "should dwell in nothing whatsoever." So when the line "should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever" is reached, the meaning of the two "should not" lines is wholly gathered within it. In short, the three lines from "should not dwell in forms" through "bring forth the mind" are all footnotes to the line "should bring forth a pure mind." Thus it is pure; not thus it is not pure. Hence it says, "should thus bring forth a pure mind."

This section's text teaches those who bring forth bodhi that they should be thus. Why does it not say "bring forth the mind" but "bring forth the mind" in the sense of generating? Let me ask: are bringing forth the mind and generating the mind the same or different? They are the same yet not the same. Generating is bringing forth; what difference is there? Hence they are the same. The sense of "generating" is deeper than the word "bringing forth." How so? "Bringing forth" speaks only of what has already become manifest and is known to others. "Generating" not only speaks of what is manifest but also carries the sense of tracing it to its source. For whenever we speak of generating, there must be a root. Without a root, how could it be generated? Thus the meaning of bringing forth the mind says that it was originally absent and is now brought forth, while the meaning of generating the mind says that it is fundamentally inherent and can be made present. Hence "generating the mind" is deeper in meaning than "bringing forth the mind"; this is their difference. How can one know that the meaning of generating the mind is like this? Looking at the three words "pure mind," one may understand. For the pure mind is precisely the fundamentally inherent nature, what is called the self-nature pure mind. "Pure" means not turbid; "clean" means not defiled. It is like true gold fallen into the mud: apply effort and wash it, and the true gold is still there. The nature is likewise so. Though it has all along been obscured by the dust and defilement of ignorance and affliction, if one can cultivate according to the Dharma, the pure original nature will still appear. Therefore the meaning of this line is that all who bring forth the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment mind should cause the pure original nature to appear. Hence it says, "should bring forth a pure mind." There is a sense in these words of "turn the head and the shore is there"; how deeply it warns people. Nor is this all. It shows that the thousand words and ten thousand phrases that came before, saying one should not dwell in marks, were nothing but a wish to enable one to see the nature. Purity is the meaning of being without marks. Ordinary beings cling to marks and thereby obstruct the nature. Now if one wishes to see the nature, how can one cling to marks? Ordinary beings cling to marks, and so are impure. The mind being impure, the nature is obstructed. Now if one wishes to see the nature, one should be pure. To purify the mind, one should be free from marks. Moreover, to speak of bringing forth a pure mind is no different from explaining the reason for bringing forth the bodhi mind. What is called bringing forth the bodhi mind? It is the one mind being pure. If the mind is not pure, could what is brought forth still be called unsurpassed bodhi? Why? Bodhi means enlightenment. Enlightenment means illuminating the original nature. The original nature is also called the ocean of the great perfect enlightenment. One should know that the original nature is untouched by a single speck of dust, incomparably pure. If one speaks of awakening and yet clings to marks, one runs directly counter to the word "enlightenment." Such a one is what is called an ordinary being who turns his back on enlightenment and joins with dust. Therefore one who brings forth the enlightenment mind must join with enlightenment. How does one join with enlightenment? One must turn the back on dust. Turning the back on dust means not dwelling in marks. Seen in this light, this one line contains countless urgings and warnings.

When one has just brought forth the bodhi mind, how can the pure mind at once appear? One should know that precisely because one cannot, one is taught to cultivate thus. How does one cultivate? It is what the text below calls dwelling in nothing whatsoever. How does one dwell in nothing whatsoever? It is what the text below calls not dwelling in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas. This plainly shows the method of applying effort in non-dwelling. The two lines on not dwelling in forms are deep and broad in meaning; if one merely glances at them and understands only one sense, one truly fails them. Moreover, if the meanings are not fully explored, how can one's effort be to the point, be practical, be fine? If one works only on the surface, how can marks be left behind, and how can the nature be seen? Hence it is said one fails them. One not only fails the Buddha's kindness; one fails one's own nature.

(1) These forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas are called the six objects. They are brought up here to make one understand that if one clings to even one of them, it is a mind of dust. This is precisely the opposite of the pure mind. Therefore one who brings forth the mind of right enlightenment must turn the back on dust, and having turned the back on dust, join with enlightenment. Not dwelling in the six objects is like saying one should not join with dust, for joining with dust is turning the back on enlightenment. The workings of this leave no room for a hair. It is truly what is called "the human mind is precarious, the mind of the Way is subtle."

(2) Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas are what is called the world of vessels, also called the marks of the realm. Now it says one should not dwell in these six; this is the meaning of not dwelling in marks. The five words forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects include all the realms in the world that can be seen and heard. The one word "dharmas" includes all the realms in the world that cannot be seen or heard but can be reached by thought. Bringing up these six words gathers in all the marks of the realms, that is, all realms in the world are not to be clung to. Not only should what can be seen and heard not be clung to; what cannot be seen or heard should likewise not be clung to. This is to instruct and warn students that in the world, nothing at all should be clung to.

(3) What should not be clung to is not only the realms. On the surface it speaks only of the six objects, but in fact the six faculties and the six consciousnesses are all spoken of together within it. If one looks only at the surface, as was said above of working merely on the pure surface, then the work of the two words "not dwelling" cannot be thorough, nor can it be to the point. Though one wishes not to dwell, one cannot attain it. One should know that forms are an outer realm, fundamentally without any involvement. Involvement arises from dwelling. Who is it that dwells? The eye. How does the eye dwell? Through eye-consciousness. And so on to dharmas, which are inert things: if one does not dwell and cling, there is no relation at all. That a relation arises is due, to be sure, to the mind; but in fact it is due to the consciousness within the mind that is habituated to seeking and discriminating. From this one may know that when the sutra says one should not dwell, it is telling students to illuminate and observe at the level of consciousness, and not to give rise to seeking and discriminating. The sutra not only says one should not dwell in forms, nor in sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas; it also attaches the two words "bring forth the mind" after them, precisely to show students that if they wish not to dwell in marks, they should illuminate and observe in the mind. That is, they should apply effort finely and secretly at the moment when the mind stirs and thoughts arise. Only thus is it practical.

(4) To apply effort at the moment when the mind stirs and thoughts arise is the point of entry for beginners, but one must also cut off one's deluded cravings. How does one cut them off? By bringing forth the great compassionate mind and widely cultivating the six pāramitās. Giving and keeping the precepts counter greed; keeping the precepts and patience counter hatred, and also counter pride; prajñā counters delusion; dhyāna, since it counters hatred, and since concentration can give rise to wisdom, also counters delusion. And all of it is pervaded by the spirit of diligence. Moreover, since the six pāramitās all come forth from the great compassionate mind, every pāramitā benefits beings. This is again a sharp weapon for removing the self. For it is because of the view of self that greed, hatred, delusion, and pride arise, and so thoughts easily stir. Now if one wishes not to let thoughts stir on account of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas, one must intensify one's effort in the great compassionate mind and the practice of the six pāramitās. Only thus is it to the point.

(5) As said above, it is still not ultimate. One must make precepts and concentration firm and bring forth the right wisdom of prajñā. When ignorance is broken by one part, consciousness turns by one part. Only when all eight consciousnesses have turned is it thorough. Beginners must read many Great Vehicle scriptures, and prajñā above all must not be parted from for even a moment. Relying on the words to give rise to contemplation, one causes the wisdom of understanding gradually to grow clear. This is precisely the method of pulling the firewood out from under the pot. And as the wisdom of understanding grows clear, it can further increase the power of precepts and concentration. For though precepts, concentration, and wisdom are called the three trainings, they are in fact one matter, with the wonder of mutually aiding and producing one another. And concentration and wisdom above all cannot be separated: concentration certainly produces wisdom, and wisdom also produces concentration. This meaning one must not fail to know.

(6) The two words "bring forth the mind" not only tell one to apply effort at the moment when the mind stirs and thoughts arise; they contain a deeper meaning still. This guards against those who do not understand the method of applying effort and who, misunderstanding the meaning of "should not dwell," single-mindedly suppress consciousness and prevent it from arising. Practicing thus, the impatient are sure to go mad or vomit blood. Even if not, it is what Chan masters revile as "sitting inside a black mountain ghost cave making a living," no different from the non-perception meditations of the outsiders. Since the principle is not clear, (not knowing that the original nature is lively and alive, neither with marks nor without marks, is what is meant by the principle not being clear) wisdom cannot arise, delusion cannot be removed, and the suffering of karma certainly cannot be dissolved. One may even turn into an insentient thing of grass, wood, earth, or stone. One should know that the Small Vehicle's meditation of extinction is not attained by suppressing consciousness, but by realizing the nature, whereupon thoughts do not arise of themselves. And even at this stage one should not dwell. To dwell is to fall into the pit of the unconditioned, a scorched sprout and rotten seed, which the World-Honored One also reviles. Therefore the sutra text says both "do not dwell in forms and the rest" and "bring forth the mind." It shows that one who brings forth the bodhi mind should not dwell in the marks of dust, but is not told to make the mind like dead water. This meaning exactly echoes the line below, "should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever." It instructs students both clearly and to the point.

(7) Not dwelling in the six objects while bringing forth the mind has yet another meaning. Joined with the line above, it tells one who brings forth bodhi and cultivates the six pāramitās to distinguish the true mind from the deluded mind. The "pure mind" of the line above is the true mind. These two lines, dwelling in dust, describe the seeking mind, which is the deluded mind. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: "All beings, from beginningless time, have had all sorts of inversion, and all practitioners cannot attain unsurpassed bodhi; some even become hearers, solitary realizers, or outsiders, all because they do not know the two roots and so cultivate in confusion. The first is the root of beginningless birth and death: it is that you and all beings now take the seeking mind as your own nature. The second is the beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa, the originally pure essence: it is that you now, with the essential brightness of consciousness, can produce all conditions, and what is left behind by conditions." Here the line above says "should," and the two lines below say "should not," precisely and intimately showing that one must not cultivate in confusion. One should know that the mind dwelling in dust is consciousness. Because it seeks, it is called deluded. Yet this deluded mind is originally a transformation of the true mind. How does it transform? Because it does not penetrate the one true dharma-realm and so discriminates between self and others. Therefore one who brings forth the great mind must first distinguish the true from the deluded. One should not take the mind that dwells in dust and clings to marks as the true mind. That is why this sutra lays such stress on breaking the self. "Should not dwell in the six objects while bringing forth the mind" means one should not cling to self. Why is clinging to dust the same as clinging to self? For example, one who practices the six pāramitās, if his intention is to be known by others, is dwelling in forms, and so on to clinging to dharmas. All such things are nothing but the view of self. These two lines are spoken precisely to call forth the line below.

"Dwell in nothing whatsoever" also has several meanings. (1) It means dwelling in nothing among the six objects. (2) It means that faculties, objects, and consciousness are all not dwelt in. Whatever it may be that one dwells in and clings to, the mind becomes defiled, and that is a mark of dust. (3) "Nothing whatsoever" means not dwelling in anything at all. (4) "Nothing whatsoever" means having nothing dwelt in. What is dwelt in is forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas. Now it says one should have nothing dwelt in within the mind; it does not say there are no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas. It contains two senses: not clinging, and also not annihilating. Again, the absence of what is dwelt in is due to the emptiness of the one who dwells. "What is dwelt in" refers to the object; "the one who dwells" refers to consciousness. Hence "should dwell in nothing whatsoever" is like saying one should cause emotional consciousness to be wholly emptied.

The word "and" in "and bring forth the mind" has two meanings. (1) "And" means "and again." One should dwell in nothing whatsoever, and again bring forth the mind. This carries on the earlier teaching of dwelling in nothing whatsoever, together with the sense of not annihilating, and speaks from there. That is, it explains that what was said above, "should not dwell in the six objects while bringing forth the mind," means that in the mind there should be no marks of forms, sounds, and the rest that are dwelt in; it does not mean the mark of annihilation. "Not annihilating" is because the mind cannot be annihilated. What was said above, that one should not dwell in dust while bringing forth the mind, is to cause one to dwell in nothing whatsoever and bring forth the mind. The word "the" may refer to bodhi and to the six pāramitās. Thus the mind that brings forth the cultivation of the six pāramitās is then a bodhi mind, because it turns the back on dust and leaves marks behind, in accord with the self-nature pure mind. (2) "And" means "and then." This carries on the earlier teaching that one should dwell in nothing whatsoever, which is like saying one should cause emotional consciousness to be wholly emptied. Then "the mind" refers to purity. It means that dwelling in nothing whatsoever causes one's delusion to be exhausted and the mind of thoughts to be empty, and only then can one's pure mind appear. "Bring forth" means to make present. For the line "should bring forth a pure mind" is the topic stated. The two "should not" lines are the method of cultivation. The line "should dwell in nothing whatsoever" is the effect. One must explain it in all these ways before the sutra's meaning feels somewhat clear and complete — and even then it is but a drop in the great ocean. The explanation of the meaning according to the text above is now complete.

The explanation of the meaning according to the text above is now complete. How is this the spot where the eye is dotted and the vital point tied for all that was said before? Let us proceed layer by layer in reverse. Did not the section above say "is not" and "is called"? The reason for these four characters was not yet revealed in the section above, and so it closely carries on that meaning and makes it clear. Thus the two words "thus" may be said to carry on directly from "is not" and "is called." It means that one who brings forth the great Way mind adorns the Buddha-lands, and should contemplate the meaning of "is not" and "is called" and bring forth a pure mind. For the line "is not" makes clear that one should dwell in nothing whatsoever. Why? What is brought forth is originally without marks. In adorning, one's mind should dwell in nothing at all among marks such as the six objects; hence "is not." Knowing "is not," the mind is pure. This is what is called: if one wishes to purify the Buddha-land, one should purify one's mind. The line "is called" makes clear that one should bring forth the mind. Why? The mind should simply not dwell in marks, but this is not to annihilate the marks. Hence "is called." "Is called" means that the name is correct and the words are fitting; the affair cannot be abolished. One should know that the marks of the affair of adorning cannot be annihilated. That is, the mind of adorning has never at any point ceased; and if the mind has not ceased, that is bringing forth the mind. In short, if one adorns while the mind does not dwell in marks, then while blazingly adorning, the mind is nonetheless deep, still, and unmoved, unstained by a speck of dust. Though it is called bringing forth the mind, in truth it brings forth without bringing forth, the one mind pure. Hence it says, "should thus bring forth a pure mind." The mind pure, the land pure. This is what is called: as the mind becomes pure, so the Buddha-land becomes pure. Thus, thus, does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-lands. This is the model for one who brings forth the great Way mind, cultivates the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices, and adorns the Buddha-lands.

The section above on generating faith has two essential lines: "should not grasp dharmas, should not grasp non-dharmas." These two lines not only gather in the meaning of the section above; they also gather in the meaning of the entire sutra, as has been said repeatedly. And here the "should bring forth a pure mind" and "should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever" are again the spot where the eye is dotted for those two lines. For the two lines of the section above were spoken separately. Here the meaning of the two lines is joined into one and spoken. How so? "Should dwell in nothing whatsoever" is "should not grasp dharmas." "Bring forth the mind" is "should not grasp non-dharmas." Now it says, "should dwell in nothing whatsoever and bring forth the mind." Is this not to say that though one should not grasp dharmas, one should also not grasp non-dharmas? The earlier words, that not grasping dharmas should take not grasping non-dharmas as its boundary, are precisely what is understood from this point. And the reason only those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit are singled out as able to generate faith is also that they certainly will not grasp the mark of non-dharmas, and so are fit to cultivate this mark-free prajñā. From this one may see that we must first shut the side of the mark of non-dharmas tight, absolutely not grasping it. Only then, cultivating the non-grasping of the mark of dharmas, does one accord with the Buddha's intent, bring forth the right wisdom of prajñā, and realize the principle-essence of prajñā. Nor is this all. Consider the line "should bring forth a pure mind." Purity is precisely dwelling in nothing whatsoever. "Should bring forth a pure mind" is like saying one should bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever. And dwelling in nothing whatsoever is not grasping dharmas. Bringing forth the mind is not grasping non-dharmas. "Should bring forth a pure mind" says that purity must appear within the bringing forth of the mind. (But purity without bringing forth the mind is dead water, which the Buddhadharma does not permit.) Is this not to say that not grasping dharmas must be carried out within not grasping non-dharmas?

In other words, not grasping dharmas is emptiness; not grasping non-dharmas is existence. "Dwelling in nothing whatsoever and bringing forth the mind" makes clear that emptiness does not depart from existence. "Bringing forth a pure mind" makes clear that emptiness is within existence. Emptiness not departing from existence is like saying form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. Not departing and not different gradually merge; yet emptiness is still emptiness, and existence still existence, so they are still one and yet two. If emptiness appears within existence, then form is precisely emptiness and emptiness is precisely form. Emptiness and existence being identical, they are two and yet one. This is called the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. One must be able to be thus before one is free of both sides. Why? There is not yet any such thing as two; from where could one cling to a side? Nor is this all. Since it says "dwell in nothing whatsoever," and also says "bring forth the mind," is it not that dwelling in nothing whatsoever should also not be dwelt in? And the two words "pure" and "clean" in "should bring forth a pure mind" are precisely what is called dwelling in nothing whatsoever. Then "bringing forth a pure mind" is no different from saying "bringing forth the non-dwelling mind." Though it brings forth, it does not dwell; this makes clear that its bringing forth is no bringing forth, that is, it does not dwell in bringing forth the mind. Not dwelling in bringing forth the mind is not dwelling in not grasping non-dharmas. And not dwelling in dwelling in nothing whatsoever is also not dwelling in not grasping dharmas. Is this not that not grasping both sides should also not be grasped? Hence in the section above, following "not grasping both sides," the raft simile is cited to make clear that both sides are to be let go. Above, the simultaneity of emptiness and existence made clear that there is not yet any two, so there is no side to cling to. Yet one may still cling to the one. (Clinging to the one is what is called the mere middle.) Now emptiness and existence are both empty, and the one does not remain either; what is there to cling to? Unobstructed and at ease, this is true purity. The true meaning of the two lines "should not grasp dharmas" is here unfolded thoroughly, and so it is called dotting the eye. As for "no marks of dharmas and also no marks of non-dharmas," that is precisely "should dwell in nothing whatsoever and bring forth the mind." "Non-dharmas and not non-dharmas" is precisely the pure mind in which emptiness and existence are both empty, that is, the unconditioned Dharma. When emptiness and existence are both empty, mental activity ceases and the path of words is cut off; hence it is called ungraspable and unutterable. All this is plain and evident and needs no further words.

The section above also has an essential line: "If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata." The reason for this is likewise made clear here. If all marks are no marks, how can one see? If one's mind is defiled by dust and turned away from enlightenment, one is just then deluded into taking marks as real; how could one see all marks as no marks? One must dwell in nothing at all among marks such as the six objects, and only when the mind is pure is it at all possible. Why? The Tathāgata is one who has already ultimately realized the pure mind. One who does not dwell in the six objects, though he cannot be said to have realized it, yet as the dregs gradually settle, the pure light appears. It is like pure water that can reflect the pure moon. Hence it says, "then one sees the Tathāgata."
