For the Tathāgata is the title of the essence of the nature; one must not cling to marks and instead illuminate the essence, and only then can one see it.

Did not the section above say at its opening: "A bodhisattva should practice giving while dwelling in no dharma"? It did explain that not dwelling in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas is giving that does not dwell in marks. Yet when one brings forth the mind to give, that mind must not be one that arises dwelling on the six objects; only then, in the act, can one not dwell in marks. If the mind is impure, how can one not cling to marks in the act? From this one may know that what is said here speaks precisely at the source. Though what the section above said did contain the sense of the mind, and it later pointed this out with the words "if the mind grasps marks" and so on, in fact it is only here that it is unfolded and made clear. Without this passage, giving that does not dwell in marks would not easily be grasped. Hence it is said that this section is the spot where the eye is dotted and the vital point tied for all the meanings above. Once the eye is dotted, the whole body comes alive. Once the vital point is tied, all the vessels flow toward it. Then a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, each and every one, have a place to land. And in practicing according to the teaching, every matter has something to hold to.

In sum, if one understands the true meaning of dwelling in nothing whatsoever and bringing forth the mind, then what is called bringing forth is bringing forth spontaneously, and what is called non-dwelling may as well dwell as conditions allow. To dwell as conditions allow is to have no mind for dwelling; though one dwells, one in truth dwells in nothing. To bring forth spontaneously is to manifest naturally; though called bringing forth, one in truth brings forth nothing. If one can be thus, then every dharma reveals the non-dwelling true mind, and every thing is none other than the true mark of prajñā. This is precisely what the ancients called "every mote of dust is a treasure; everywhere one meets him." That is why I, Subhūti, when the World-Honored One was putting on his robe, begging for food, walking, sitting, and coming and going, perceived the wondrous truth of non-dwelling, and at once rose from my seat among the assembly, bowed, and praised him, saying: "Rare indeed, World-Honored One, well guarding in thought, well entrusting." And I asked, for one who brings forth the great mind, how should he dwell, how should he subdue? The World-Honored One met the occasion and confirmed it, saying: as you have said of well guarding in thought and well entrusting, so should one dwell, so should one subdue. Below he speaks of it again in detail, like a thousand cliffs and ten thousand gorges winding and stretching, until here it is tied up, saying: "should thus bring forth a pure mind, bring forth the mind that dwells in nothing whatsoever." "Should bring forth a pure mind" is what is called "should thus dwell." "Should dwell in nothing whatsoever and bring forth the mind" is what is called "thus subdue the mind." Only when one is woken by the one "thus" here do the two "thus" of the opening general instruction have a place to land. That is, the two "thus" above gain this one "thus," and their meaning becomes more intimate and more thorough. To call it a distant echo is still one layer off; it is simply fused into one flavor. Hence these two-odd lines of this section are a great tying of the vital point from the opening of the sutra to here. It is like a geomancer: through a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters he traces the dragon vein everywhere. If he cannot find the true vital point, he will inevitably set foot on a side branch and fail to grasp the essentials. But if he finds the true vital point, then the sand, the water, the green dragon, and the white tiger are all at his service. The student of Buddhism is likewise so. In studying Buddhism one must practice according to the teaching; the teaching's meaning is deep and hidden, and one must grasp where its essentials lie. And this passage is the essential outline of all the meanings stated before. One should, in regard to "should not dwell in forms and bring forth the mind, should not dwell in sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas and bring forth the mind," know thus, see thus, believe thus, and understand thus. Whatever dharma one cultivates, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one does not part from this. Only then does the principle of non-dwelling have a place of entry, and only then can the self-nature pure mind gradually give a hint of itself. And the dharma one cultivates may also be hoped to reach accomplishment. A thousand times, ten thousand times. Again, since this passage is the essential outline of all that came before, if one understands this outline and practices giving and the other dharmas by it, then everything one does is the Way. That is why in the next section, comparing and revealing the sutra's merit, the merit and virtue are greater than that of generating faith by who knows how many times.
(Gui) 3. Confirming by the non-dwelling of the reward body.

["Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body were like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. What do you think? Is that body great?" Subhūti said, "Very great, World-Honored One. Why? The Buddha says it is no body; therefore it is called a great body."]

"Suppose" is a simile. Every simile serves to confirm what is said of the Dharma. Though the teaching of the Dharma above has been fully unfolded, now it is again confirmed by a simile for no other reason than that the hearer may understand still more clearly. "A person" secretly points to one who brings forth the great Way mind. The great mind is the cause; the great body is the fruition. Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, stands for the surpassing, wondrous reward body. This body is subtle; though it has form and marks, only bodhisattvas on the grounds can see it. It is precisely by diligently cultivating the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices through many kalpas, adorning both merit and wisdom, and perfecting one's practice, that one can realize it: what is called the body of boundless marks and excellences. If one doubts that the marks of the surpassing, wondrous reward body are unlike ordinary marks, and thinks that if this is not grasped, then what is the use of cultivating the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices? Such a one does not understand that whether fruition stage or causal ground, marks and no marks are all not to be grasped. If one's understanding of this principle is even slightly unclear, then in cultivating the cause one cannot deeply accord with "should dwell in nothing whatsoever and bring forth the mind." This is the subtle intent of the Buddha's question. Subhūti deeply understood the Buddha's intent, and so at once answered, "Very great." Saying "very great" makes clear that this body is not nonexistent; it is no different from first giving a calming pill to the doubtful, so that they may know that to bring forth a great vow and cultivate a great practice will surely attain a surpassing, wondrous great body — truly not deceptive. "Why?" asks: by what cause does one attain this great body? "Buddha" is the title of fruition virtue. "No body" has two senses. (1) Speaking in terms of the realized fruition, what is realized is the essence of the pure dharma-body, not the marks of this reward body. Then "no body" refers to the reward body. (2) Speaking in terms of the realized fruition, since it is the essence of the dharma-body, and this dharma-body encompasses the sand-realm all around (its greatness has no outside) and enters every mote of dust (its smallness has no inside), it has no form and no measure. Hence the Vimalakīrti Sutra says the Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any category. The sense is that speaking in terms of the essence, it is said to be no body. Then "no body" refers to the dharma-body. "Is called a great body" refers to the reward body, making clear the surpassing, wondrous, tall and great reward body. The sense is that speaking in terms of marks, it is said to be very great. "Is called" means name and mark. The sense is: speaking in terms of the realized dharma-body, it is truly the formless no-body; how could greatness or smallness be spoken of? To say "very great" now is spoken in terms of the name and marks of the reward body. One who attains the fruit, though he does not lack these tall and great marks, in truth keeps no notion of attainment. To keep a notion of attainment is to dwell in the marks of the body. If one dwells in the marks of the body, how can one be said to realize the pure, markless dharma-body? If the dharma-body is not realized, there is no very great reward body either. If one understands this principle, one knows that one should not grasp the marks of the body, yet this surpassing reward is not nonexistent. One who can cultivate the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices without grasping will realize the pure dharma-body, and all surpassing marks will naturally appear. One need not cling to existence, nor cling to nothingness. Then in cultivating the cause one can avoid grasping the mark of self and not dwell in the six objects, and so bring forth the pure mind.

(Ren) 2. Comparing and revealing by way of the sutra's merit. It divides into two: (Gui) 1. Revealing the surpassing merit and virtue; 2. Revealing why it surpasses. (Gui) 1. Again divides into three: (Zi) 1. Citing the simile of the Ganges' sands; 2. Making clear the merit of giving material things; 3. Revealing the superiority of upholding the sutra.
(Zi) 1. Citing the simile of the Ganges' sands.

["Subhūti, as many as all the sands in the Ganges River, and as many Ganges Rivers as there are sands — what do you think? Are all those Ganges Rivers' sands many?" Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. Even the Ganges Rivers alone are countless in number; how much more their sands."]

In India there is a great river called the Ganges. The sound "Ganges" is slightly corrupted; it should be Gaṅgā, which is translated as the River of Merit. This river in India is like the Yellow River and the Yangtze in China, irrigating the whole country and bringing great benefit to transport, planting, commerce, and culture; hence it is called the River of Merit. Also, the people of ancient India regarded it as sacred water: to see this river, or to bathe in it, brings immeasurable merit. So it is also translated as "come from heaven," because its source is high. China too has the line, "the waters of the Yellow River come from heaven." The Buddhist sutras say: north of Jambudvīpa there are nine black mountains, then the great Snow Mountain, and then the Fragrant Drunken Mountain. South of the Fragrant and north of the Snow is a lake named Anavatapta, which means "free from the fever of affliction." The lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, filled with the water of eight excellent qualities. The lake has four mouths, and from each mouth comes a river; the rushing waters flow into the sea, each dividing into twenty-five thousand great rivers. Together they irrigate the four continents. What comes from the eastern mouth is the Gaṅgā, which enters the southeastern sea. The southern mouth gives the Indus, which enters the southwestern sea. The western mouth gives the Vakṣu, which enters the northwestern sea. The northern mouth gives the Sītā, which enters the northeastern sea.

The sands of the Ganges are extremely fine, and the finer they are, the more their number is seen to be. Hence in the Buddhist sutras, whenever a number too great to calculate is spoken of, the sands of the Ganges are used as a simile. And because everyone in India knew this river and knew that the number of sands in it could not be calculated, the river's sands are used as a simile because they were understood by all. The word "as" in "as the Ganges" means "for example," and its force carries down into the phrase below, "as many Ganges Rivers as there are sands." "As many Ganges Rivers as there are sands" means taking all the sands now in the Ganges and turning each grain into a new river. The number of the original sands being immeasurable, the new Ganges Rivers equal to them are likewise immeasurable in number. Hence it says, "as many Ganges Rivers as there are sands." It is like saying: suppose all the immeasurable sands in the present Ganges were turned into immeasurable new Ganges Rivers equal in number to those immeasurable sands. "All those Ganges Rivers": "those" means these; "all" means immeasurable. The question asks whether the sands in these immeasurable new Ganges Rivers can be called many. The answer, "very many," makes clear that they are so many as to be unutterable. The lines following "even the" mean that even speaking of the new Ganges Rivers alone, they are already countless and incalculable; how much more the sands within them, whose number is still more boundless and beyond description, so that one can only say vaguely, "very many."
(Zi) 2. Making clear the merit of giving treasures.

["Subhūti, I now tell you in truth: if a good man or good woman were to fill as many trichiliocosms as there are sands in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and give them away, would the merit attained be great?" Subhūti said, "Very great, World-Honored One."]

"I tell you in truth": the words are spoken here, but the intent rests on the section below, so that one may know that the merit of upholding and teaching spoken of below is greater than this, is true speech, and must be believed. The old phrase "so many" is what writers today call "such an amount." "Such an amount" is a pointing word, like the Shanghai saying "that many" or the northern saying "this much."

The Ganges is immeasurable and its sands boundless. "As many as the sands of those Ganges Rivers" is like saying immeasurable and boundless. Subhūti deeply understood the Buddha's intent and knew that all that had been said above was nothing but borrowing the extremely great merit and virtue of conditioned dharmas to make a comparison, in order to reveal that the unconditioned Dharma of upholding and teaching has merit and virtue still greater than this. The intent was never in this. Hence he answered only, "Very great," without adding other words.
(Zi) 3. Revealing the superiority of upholding the sutra.

[The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a good man or good woman, within this sutra, should receive and uphold even a four-line verse and teach it to others, that merit and virtue would surpass the former merit and virtue."]

The meaning of receiving and upholding, and of the four-line verse, has already been fully explained. "Even a four-line verse" speaks of upholding and teaching the very least of the sutra, and its merit and virtue still surpass the former. Then upholding and teaching the whole sutra has merit and virtue still greater; this needs no saying. Receiving and upholding, one can save oneself. Teaching it to others, one can save others. Saving oneself and saving others is bodhisattva practice. Hence the merit and virtue are extremely great. That the merit and virtue of upholding the sutra and teaching the Dharma surpasses that of giving has a general and a particular sense. The general sense is that no matter what sutra one upholds, no matter what Dharma one teaches, it is always so. The particular sense is that this is said specifically of this sutra.

First let us make clear the general sense. Speaking in terms of saving oneself: if in giving one does not know how to leave marks behind, then even when the merit and virtue are great to the utmost, it is no more than rebirth in heaven. Hence it is called outflows merit and virtue. That is, it is still leaking and falling into the path of birth and death and rebirth; one cannot speak of saving oneself. But if one can receive and uphold the sutra's meaning, one can open wisdom, can know that rebirth is fearsome and seek to escape it. And when practicing giving, one also knows to leave marks behind. Then one cultivates both merit and wisdom, can reach the other shore, end birth and death, and realize the sage's fruit. Compared with that one who can only be reborn in heaven and still cannot escape rebirth, the distance is as heaven from an abyss. Therefore, though one receives and upholds only a single four-line verse, its merit already surpasses the giving of treasures filling immeasurable, boundless great trichiliocosms — how much more for one who receives and upholds the whole sutra!

Speaking in terms of saving others: the giving of wealth is not equal to the giving of Dharma, and this contains many meanings; let me briefly explain them. (1) In the giving of wealth, giver and receiver do not necessarily have wisdom. In the giving of Dharma, without wisdom one cannot give it, and without wisdom one cannot receive it. (2) In the giving of wealth, the giver gains great merit but the receiver gains only a small present benefit. In the giving of Dharma, both giver and receiver gain great merit. (3) The giving of wealth benefits only a person's life; the giving of Dharma benefits a person's wisdom-life. (4) The giving of wealth subdues greed; the giving of Dharma cuts off delusion. (5) In the giving of wealth, both sides do not escape rebirth; in the giving of Dharma, both sides can end birth and death. (6) In the giving of wealth, the enjoyment of both sides is exhaustible; in the giving of Dharma, the enjoyment of both sides is inexhaustible. (7) In the giving of wealth, if one gives little, the benefit is little; in the giving of Dharma, one may give little and gain great benefit. Question: then may one practice only the giving of Dharma and not the giving of wealth? Answer: no. When a bodhisattva gathers and receives beings, the giving of wealth also cannot be lacking. But the aim lies in practicing the giving of Dharma, and the giving of wealth is not taken as ultimate. The above makes clear in general the benefit to self and other of upholding and teaching all sutras and dharmas. The section below specifically makes clear the benefit of upholding and teaching this sutra. One should know that the Diamond Prajñā points directly at the original nature. If one can see the nature, one can become a Buddha. Not only does one end one's own birth and death and cause beings to end birth and death; one can directly deliver immeasurable, boundless beings and cause them all to become Buddhas. To continue and prosper the Buddha-seed, nothing surpasses this sutra. The greatness of its merit and virtue is inconceivable, and how could it merely surpass the merit and virtue of the former giving of treasures filling boundless great trichiliocosms?

inline.s: (Gui) 2. Revealing why it surpasses. It divides into two: (Zi) 1. Making clear the merit of teaching as occasion arises; 2. Making clear the merit of upholding it fully.
(Zi) 1. Making clear the merit of teaching as occasion arises.

["Again, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is taught as occasion arises, even a four-line verse, one should know that that place — all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras — should all make offerings to it as to a Buddha's stūpa and temple."]

Whenever it says "again," though it cites another meaning, it in fact accomplishes the former meaning; this has been explained in detail above. "As occasion arises" carries the sense of not being fixed, and to speak briefly there are five aspects. "According to the person," whether monastic or lay, sage or ordinary. "According to capacity," whether of sharp or dull faculties. (This is the sense of teaching the shallow and the deep in turn, now speaking the ultimate meaning, now the antidote.) "According to the text," whether much or little, broad or brief. "According to the place," whether city or countryside, noble or lowly. "According to the time," whether day or night, long or short. "According to the assembly," whether many people or one. Whenever a fitting opportunity for teaching is met, one teaches it. This is what is called teaching as occasion arises. "One should know" warns that it must not be slighted. Here it refers to the place where the sutra is taught; if the place of teaching is thus, the teacher may be known. The section below says, "one should know that such a person" and so on. So we know that speaking of the place, it also speaks of the person. In short, one who hears the sutra must not fail to keep a mind of reverence. Why? Because one venerates the Dharma and does not forget where it came from. But one who teaches the sutra must not keep this mind. Why? Because one keeps far from fame, profit, and reverence, and should not cling to marks. Both sides should know this. Again, the Great Prajñā Sutra says: Indra every day in the Hall of Good Dharma taught the prajñā-pāramitā Dharma to the assembled gods. When sometimes he was absent and the gods came, they would bow and make offerings toward the empty seat and then leave. This is the fact that the gods, following the Buddha's teaching, revered the place where the sutra was taught. Again, the Great Compilation says: the gods make reverence three times a day, and still more on the six fast days. Wherever the sutra is, all four sides are to be made pure.

"The world" is like saying "the cosmos." "Between" carries the sense of interval. As when one says "one room," it makes clear the boundaries of the room. If it had no boundaries, how could it be called one room? Hence to say "the world" is no different from saying "the cosmos." "World" carries the vertical sense: thirty years make one generation. "Realm" carries the horizontal sense: each direction and each place has its own boundary. Now it says "all the world," making clear that vertically it reaches to the end of the future and horizontally it extends through the ten directions. That is, it is the sense of exhausting the future and pervading the dharma-realm.

To speak of gods and humans is to gather in all beings of the three realms. And to speak of gods and asuras is to gather in the eight classes of gods and dragons. Hence though three are named, all are included. The two words "should all" exactly echo "one should know." How should one know? Because all should. "Should" means it cannot be otherwise; hence one should know.

There are two kinds of offering. (1) Offering of affairs, briefly stated in ten items: incense, flowers, necklaces of gems, powdered incense, rubbed incense, burned incense, banners and canopies, clothing, music and dance, and joining the palms in bowing. The place where the sutra is taught is a place of the Way, and so it should be adorned and revered in this way. (2) Offering of Dharma, which is cultivating according to the Dharma and benefiting beings (such as hearing it and in turn teaching it to others, or giving the sutra away as a gift, and so on), gathering and receiving beings (such as urging people to come and listen, sharing one's seat with others, and so on), even not abandoning the bodhisattva's work (such as coming to listen even when meeting obstacles, which is not abandoning it), and not departing from the bodhi mind (such as bringing forth great vows and great practices without violating the right wisdom of prajñā. "Not departing" means not contradicting the sutra's purport), and so on.

"As to a Buddha's stūpa and temple" means that all should make offerings to it as one makes offerings to a Buddha's stūpa and temple. That one makes offerings to a stūpa and temple is known to all. The place where the sutra is taught is sometimes neglected. Hence the stūpa and temple are cited as an example, to make clear that the place of teaching the sutra is a place of the Way, no different at all from a stūpa or temple, and so all should make offerings to it. (Why is it a place of the Way? The text below makes this even more solemnly clear.) All of this is to make clear that the teacher of the Dharma is one sent by the Buddha, and the Dharma he teaches is originally what the Buddha taught. Hence in proclaiming it on the Buddha's behalf, he is the same as the Buddha being present. The Lotus Sutra says: "If one can teach the Lotus Sutra, even a single line, to one person, such a one is sent by the Tathāgata and does the Tathāgata's work." If this is so of the Lotus Sutra, it is so of all sutras, and of the Diamond Prajñā most of all. The words above, "one should know," point to this. If one knows that such a person is sent by the Buddha and that the Dharma is spoken by the Buddha, one knows of oneself that all should be revered and offered to.

Stūpa is Sanskrit; in full it is stūpa, the sound slightly corrupted, and it is in fact stupa. Its meaning is "a high and conspicuous place"; it is also translated as "square tomb" or "round mound." A stūpa must be high and conspicuous, to signify what is surpassing. There are many kinds of Buddha-stūpas; let me make clear four for now: the stūpa of the place of birth, the stūpa of the attainment of the Way, the stūpa of turning the wheel of the Dharma, and the stūpa of parinirvāṇa. Now one is taught to make offerings to it as to a stūpa, and this gathers in the meaning of all four kinds. How so? This sutra makes clear the true mark. The true mark is the Buddha's dharma-body. Again it says that all Buddhas come forth from this sutra; then is this place not the stūpa of the Buddha's place of birth? One hears the Dharma and only then knows to cultivate the cause and realize the fruit. And this sutra generates immeasurable merit, dissolves all former offenses, and leads to the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi. Hence this place is the same as the stūpa of the Buddha's place of attaining the Way. To proclaim on the Buddha's behalf the Great Vehicle's most supreme Dharma: this place is precisely the stūpa of the place where the Buddha turned the wheel of the Dharma. Parinirvāṇa means the unconditioned; it also means that birth and death have ceased and that principle and affairs are ultimate. And what this sutra teaches is all the unconditioned Dharma, causing hearers to extinguish the mind of birth and death and realize the ultimate fruit, which is what is called causing them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and be delivered. To say that this place is the stūpa of the Buddha's place of parinirvāṇa — is that not also fitting?

"Temple" means "countenance." It makes clear the place where Buddha images are offered; in Sanskrit it is caitya. Every Buddha-stūpa must have the Buddha's relics offered in it. The relics are the Buddha's true body. Every temple where Buddha images are offered must have sutras and Dharma and must have the assembly of monks. To speak the one word "temple" is to speak of the place where the Three Treasures that maintain the tradition are gathered. Now it says "as to a Buddha's stūpa and temple," making clear that the teacher of the sutra proclaims on the Buddha's behalf and so is the same as the true Buddha being here. To teach this great Dharma and continue and prosper the Buddha-seed is to maintain the Three Treasures. Hence it says that to the Buddha's stūpas and temples all should make offerings. The words above, that teaching it to others surpasses the former merit and virtue, are for this reason. From this one may prove that though the sutra speaks of the place, its intent truly rests on the person. Yet such reverence is paid to the teacher of the sutra. If the teacher of the sutra teaches what is not Dharma as Dharma, or what is Dharma as not Dharma, prattling of prajñā and misteaching the Dharma and misleading people, the greatness of his offense is also beyond words. From the front side of the sutra one may see the reverse side. This again is what a teacher of the sutra should know, and should cautiously examine himself for, not slighting it in the least. Hence the text below says: "how much more one who can fully receive and uphold" and so on. "Receiving" means taking in the true meaning. "Upholding" means cultivating according to the meaning. Then if one cannot cultivate, it is a case of being able to speak but not to practice, like counting another's treasure, with not half a penny of one's own. Moreover, if one cannot cultivate, one certainly cannot take it in either. For the very deep, subtle, true meaning can certainly not be understood from the words alone. To speak without understanding will inevitably lead to prattling of prajñā and teaching prajñā shallowly. Is this not a deep, clear warning to the teacher of the sutra?
(Zi) 2. Making clear the merit of upholding it fully. It divides into two: (Chou) 1. Directly stating the full upholding; 2. Directly stating why.
(Chou) 1. Directly stating the full upholding.
["How much more one who can fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it."]

It says receiving and upholding, and then says reading and reciting, making clear that only one who can take it in and cultivate it is truly able to read and recite. Otherwise the benefit of reading and reciting is small. Moreover, since one can receive and uphold, one must also read and recite; for the sutra's meanings are inexhaustible, and reading and reciting it constantly can further perfume and increase them, so that the power of receiving and upholding advances day by day. Above it speaks of teaching; here it speaks of receiving and upholding: this is the first difference. Above it speaks of teaching as occasion arises even a four-line verse; here it speaks of fully receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting: this is the second difference. And in saying "one who," it is not necessarily the same person; it does not at first specify that this is the one who teaches the sutra. "How much more" also makes clear that one who can fully receive, uphold, read, and recite is still more surpassing than one who teaches as occasion arises. Yet the World-Honored One speaks of them separately for three reasons. First, to make clear that the merit of receiving and upholding is great, so that all may know to lay stress on this point. Second, to make clear that the ability to teach must come from the ability to receive and uphold; teaching as occasion arises must come from fully receiving and upholding. If one had not fully received and fully upheld, how could one be right on every point and teach the assembly according to time, place, capacity, and text? Third, to make clear that one who can fully receive and uphold should, whenever a fitting opportunity for teaching arises, teach it to others. It is not that fully receiving and upholding alone is more surpassing. Hence though the words above and this section differ, their meanings in fact illuminate each other. The Tathāgata's intent is truly that everyone should both be able to teach and be able to receive and uphold; both able to receive and uphold and able to teach. It cannot be divided into two, each doing one. How is this intent to be known? From the two words "accomplishment" below, one may understand. For the World-Honored One teaches this sutra and Dharma in the hope that everyone will be accomplished. And accomplishment requires saving oneself and saving others, the twofold benefit complete, before it is possible. If one only knows how to teach, or only knows how to receive and uphold, then as to benefiting others and benefiting oneself, one leans to one side; can there still be hope of accomplishment? So one knows that though the sutra's words are spoken separately, their meaning is in fact one thread. In reading the sutra and hearing the Dharma, one should not cling to the marks of words, but must understand the true meaning in this way. This is called relying on the meaning and not on the words. Again, the passage first on teaching as occasion arises is exactly the same in meaning as the opening of the sutra, which first speaks of delivering all beings without exception. The intent is to make clear that when a bodhisattva brings forth a vow, before being able to save himself he wishes first to save others. To save others is precisely to save oneself. Next, "how much more one who can fully receive and uphold" is also exactly the same in meaning as the opening of the sutra, which says, "Again, a bodhisattva should practice the six pāramitās while dwelling in no dharma." The intent is to make clear that in saving others one must still save oneself, and that saving oneself is originally for the sake of saving others. If one does not understand the meaning that self and other are not two, can one still be said to be able to receive? Can there still be any hope of accomplishment? The World-Honored One's teaching of the Dharma is like a maṇi pearl, perfect on every face. If one does not understand it thus, does one not fail this text? One should know that the texts of all sutras are stated with the utmost thoroughness and detail. It is only feared that people are rough and careless, knowing a little and understanding half, unable to empty all views and calmly comprehend. They will inevitably grasp at one side, blind to the whole, misleading themselves and others. What is called relying on the meaning teaches one that one must merge and penetrate it thoroughly and understand where its true meaning lies. And not relying on the words means that one must not, on hearing a word or half a phrase, cut off a passage and take its meaning.
(Chou) 2. Directly stating why. It divides into two: (Yin) 1. Directly revealing by way of accomplishment; 2. Concluding by way of perfuming.
(Yin) 1. Directly revealing by way of accomplishment.
["Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare Dharma."]
